W4392049920.headline: Synthetic data is not ethics-free
W4392049920.post:
Synthetic data is often presented as the way around hard data sharing, but it raises its own ethical questions that deserve serious attention.

Work by Joshi Hogenboom, Leonard Wee and Andre Dekker with colleagues.

In this commentary the authors look at synthetic data, artificially generated records that mimic real patients, as an alternative when collecting or sharing real data is not feasible or too costly. They argue that it brings distinct ethical issues of its own. [check: which issues the piece names; the stored summary is one sentence]

Why it matters: synthetic data is spreading quickly in health research, and treating it as automatically safe could hide new risks.

Limitation: this is a perspective piece, not an empirical study.

Published in EMBO Reports.

W4392946919.headline: Real-world cancer data is already usable, at every scale
W4392946919.post:
Research with real-world cancer data is already possible, from a single hospital database up to international federated studies, as long as the question matches the scale.

Work by Joshi Hogenboom, Johan van Soest and Andre Dekker with colleagues, led from the UK.

The paper reviews current real-world data resources and how researchers can get access to them: local hospital research databases, regional care records, national repositories, and federated learning for international collaboration. Case studies, mainly from the UK, show the infrastructure and governance needed at each scale.

Why it matters: real-world data can fill evidence gaps where clinical trials do not exist, and access is often named as the main barrier. The overview shows which routes exist today.

Limitation: the examples are mainly from the UK, so the governance routes may differ elsewhere.

Published in Clinical Oncology.

W4404946484.headline: Synthetic data works, but sample size changes the trade-offs
W4404946484.post:
Synthetic patient data can be useful even for a rare, varied group, but the number of real patients behind it changes its quality and privacy risk.

Work by Joshi Hogenboom, Aiara Lobo Gomes, Andre Dekker and Leonard Wee with colleagues.

From a population-based cohort of 3,735 adolescents and young adults with cancer, the team drew 13 training sets and generated synthetic data with four generators from the open-source Synthetic Data Vault. Each synthetic set was compared with its real data on veracity, utility and privacy.

All four generators produced usable data when the synthetic set was about as large as the real one. Larger synthetic sets were more faithful but generally riskier for privacy; fewer training patients sped up veracity but partly worsened privacy.

Why it matters: synthetic data is a candidate for sharing and enlarging scarce data, but only with consistent checks and a deliberate sample size.

Limitation: one cohort and generators from a single library were tested.

Published in JCO Clinical Cancer Informatics.

W7124178724.headline: Making messy cancer data talk without forcing one format
W7124178724.post:
Hospital data in different formats can be made to work together without rewriting them into one rigid standard, using knowledge graphs.

Work by Joshi Hogenboom, Varsha Gouthamchand, Andre Dekker, Leonard Wee, Johan van Soest and Aiara Lobo Gomes with colleagues in the STRONG AYA project.

STRONG AYA is building a federated data infrastructure for adolescents and young adults with cancer, a rare and scattered group whose data arrive in many formats. The team converted the structured data into linked data (RDF triples) with a semantic web tool [check: tool name, missing from the stored abstract] and used a mapping and annotation helper to query local terminologies as they are, without changing them. Graphs and mappings are published online.

Why it matters: rare-disease research needs data from many centres; this makes them reusable without every centre adopting one schema.

Limitation: this is a demonstration on the project's own data; it does not yet show results from analyses run on it.

Published in JCO Clinical Cancer Informatics.

W7128449036.headline: One patient, one knowledge graph, three hospitals that can compare
W7128449036.post:
Breast cancer records from a hospital can be turned into a validated, machine-readable "personal health knowledge graph", and registries built that way in three hospitals were interoperable.

Work by Wenjie Liang, Rutger van Mierlo, Cecile Wolfs, Andre Dekker and Petros Kalendralis with colleagues.

With patient consent, breast cancer data were extracted from the hospital systems and mapped to a reference ontology by a virtual assistant that combines classic rules with AI support. Every patient graph was checked with a SHACL validator before use, and one SPARQL query over the validated graphs produced a local breast cancer registry. The prototype runs in Maastricht and in two hospitals abroad [check: which countries].

Why it matters: keeping clinical registries up to date is slow manual work. A validated graph per patient makes secondary use across hospitals possible without re-entering data.

Limitation: this is a first prototype in three hospitals; how well the AI-supported mapping holds up at scale is not yet shown [check].

Published in npj Breast Cancer.

W7204787670.headline: Quality checks for every algorithm in a federated network
W7204787670.post:
Every algorithm that runs on the STRONG AYA federated network now goes through a defined quality assurance process.

Work by Leonard Wee and Joshi Hogenboom with colleagues in the STRONG AYA consortium.

The guidelines set out how algorithms built for Vantage6, the open-source platform that lets analyses travel to the data instead of the data travelling to the analyst, are reviewed before they are used in STRONG AYA. [check: what the review covers, e.g. code review, testing, privacy checks; the stored summary is one sentence]

Why it matters: in a federated network nobody sees the raw data, so trust rests on the algorithms themselves. A shared review process makes that trust explicit and repeatable.

W7213226988.headline: A UK cancer registry now informs young patients' care
W7213226988.post:
A regional cancer registry can feed a European data network and bring the results back into the consultation room for adolescents and young adults with cancer.

Work by Joshi Hogenboom, Varsha Gouthamchand, Aiara Lobo Gomes, Andre Dekker and Leonard Wee with colleagues in the STRONG AYA consortium and the University of Leeds.

Data from the Yorkshire Specialist Register of Cancer in Children and Young People were loaded into an open-source federated learning infrastructure, where they are analysed together with data from other consortium members without being pooled. The results flow into PROMPT, software from Leeds, and appear in the patient's electronic health record.

Why it matters: clinicians can see a patient's reported outcomes over time next to summary results from the wider consortium, which can support conversations with young patients and, later, research and policy.

Limitation: this is a proof of concept; whether it improves outcomes for young patients has not been measured yet.

Published in ESMO Real World Data and Digital Oncology.

W7218933153.headline: More diversity inside a breast tumour, less response to chemotherapy
W7218933153.post:
Across twelve studies, high or increasing intratumor heterogeneity in primary breast cancer was associated with reduced sensitivity to chemotherapy.

Work by Aria Dianati, Andre Dekker and Leonard Wee with colleagues.

The review followed PRISMA and searched MEDLINE, Web of Science and Scopus through June 2026. The twelve included studies covered triple-negative, HER2-positive and mixed cohorts, and assessed heterogeneity with genomic, transcriptomic, radiomic or immunologic methods. Proposed mechanisms behind the resistance include clonal selection, transcriptional plasticity, immune exclusion and phenotypic drift. Radiomic and MRI-derived features added predictive value beyond molecular classifiers, and combined radiomic-genomic models performed better than either alone [check: in how many of the studies].

Why it matters: heterogeneity is recognised as a core feature of breast cancer biology but is not yet used in routine care; imaging-based measures could make it usable without extra biopsies.

Limitation: twelve heterogeneous studies with different assessment methods, so no pooled effect size.

Published in Medical Oncology.

W7220851390.headline: Privacy protection that costs nothing in accuracy
W7220851390.post:
Two privacy techniques on top of federated survival analysis kept hazard ratios almost unchanged while hiding individual time-to-event data.

Work by Varsha Gouthamchand, Johan van Soest, Andre Dekker and Leonard Wee with colleagues.

In the Personal Health Train set-up, hospitals share model gradients instead of patient data, but some attacks on that infrastructure can still leak sensitive information. The study tested two protections for federated Cox proportional hazards models: grouping event times into bins so no individual time point is exposed, and local differential privacy, which adds noise to the gradients before they leave the hospital.

Both approaches reduced the privacy risk with only small variations in hazard ratios and cumulative baseline hazard curves.

Why it matters: multi-hospital survival studies can be run with a smaller re-identification risk, using methods that fit an existing federated infrastructure.

Limitation: the abstract reports the accuracy effect qualitatively; the size of the privacy gain depends on the attack model considered [check].

Published in Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics.

W7221757932.headline: AI reporting standards in health care: plenty, but none a machine can read
W7221757932.post:
Reporting standards for AI models in health care exist in numbers, but as plain text, so the information they ask for cannot be read by machines. This systematic review consolidates them.

Work by Ekaterina Akhmad, Daniel Slob, Aiara Lobo Gomes, Simone Mingels, Andre Dekker and Johan van Soest with colleagues.

Following PRISMA 2020, the team searched Scopus, Web of Science, MEDLINE, Embase, IEEE Xplore and the ACM Digital Library for standards published between 2016 and April 2026, covering structured data, images and text. Two reviewers screened independently with a third for consensus, and the included standards were analysed for the lifecycle stages they describe. [check: number of standards included and the main consolidation result; the stored abstract is cut off before the results]

Why it matters: if the items of these standards were machine-readable, model documentation could be validated and compared automatically instead of by hand.

Limitation: only open-access, English, peer-reviewed standards were included [check].

Published in JMIR AI.

W7222957496.headline: A face photo predicts survival in cancer beyond the clinical data
W7222957496.post:
A foundation model trained on more than 40 million face photographs estimated biological age with a mean error of 5.1 years and, in cancer patients, predicted survival independently of clinical factors.

Work by Leonard Nürnberg, Dennis Bontempi, Vasco Prudente, Suraj Pai and Hugo Aerts with colleagues.

FAHR-Face was fine-tuned for two tasks: age estimation on ten public image datasets, and survival prediction on 34,363 photographs of patients with cancer. Robustness to cosmetic surgery, make-up, pose and lighting was tested, as was what the model attends to. Both models were evaluated in two independent cancer cohorts with multivariable Cox models adjusted for clinical prognostic factors.

The highest-risk quartile had more than three times the mortality of the lowest (adjusted hazard ratio 3.23). Results held across age, sex, race and cancer subgroups.

Why it matters: a photograph is non-invasive and already in many patient records; the model gives a prognostic signal that clinical variables do not capture.

Limitation: validation was in cancer cohorts; use in other populations and the ethics of face-based prognosis need separate work [check].

Published in The Lancet Digital Health.
